title: Single event
text:
This is a an example of running a tiny single event FIAT model.
First of all, let’s make sure that there is some actual testdata.

! python ../../data/create_test_data.py

Now that we have some testdata, let’s take a look at the settings file.

with open("../../data/geom_event.toml", "r") as r:
    settings = r.read()
print(settings)

Now let’s execute the model!

! fiat run ../../data/geom_event.toml

Let’s take a quick look at the output.

# Import a method
from fiat.open import open_geom
from pathlib import Path

# check the output
out = open_geom(Path("../../data/output/geom_event", "spatial.gpkg"))
print(out.layer.columns)

Assert that the output is what we would expect.

assert int(out.layer[1].GetField("total_damage_1")) == 760
assert int(out.layer[3].GetField("total_damage_1")) == 1041

title: Settings
text:
The user must set the model settings in the settings.toml configuration file.
Besides the necessary/ required setttings one can set:

input in regard to the computational side of FIAT (e.g. chunking, number of threads etc),

see this page

optional/ additional input that is not necessary or more data specific,

see this page



Basic input
This section pertains to all input that is vital for running a FIAT model.
These inputs/ entries are listed in the table down below with more detailed information per entry underneath the table.






Note



File paths in the settings can be relative to the settings.toml file or absolute.





Table 1: Most basic settings file input





Entry
Type
Required
Default




type
string
Yes



output_dir
string
No
output


[hazard]





file
string
Yes



[exposure] (geom)





file
string
Yes



[exposure.variables] (geom)





vulnerability
string
Yes



[exposure] (grid)





file
string
Yes



[vulnerability]





file
string
Yes








type

type: The type of model. Choice between ‘geom’ and ‘grid’.



output_dir

output_dir: The path to the output directory.



[hazard]

file: The file path to the hazard file.



[exposure]
For the geometry model (type = "geom"), every geometry file gets its own [[exposure]] entry:

file: The path to the exposure vector file (recommended to be within the exposure directory) with the assets.
variables.vulnerability: The name of the (single) vulnerability dataset linked to this file. The [exposure.variables] table of every entry is required.

For the grid model (type = "grid"), there is a single [exposure] section:

file: The path to the exposure raster file (recommended to be within the exposure directory). The vulnerability dataset(s) of the layers are set per variable in the [[exposure.variables]] entries, see grid exposure data.



[vulnerability]

file: The path to the vulnerability NetCDF file within the vulnerability directory that contains the vulnerability datasets. Only one vulnerability file is allowed.







Note



The calculation method is set per vulnerability dataset (the method of the [[vulnerability.variables]] settings), see methods. There is no global method setting.


The variables (datasets, bands and layers) of the vulnerability, hazard and (gridded) exposure data can be further specified with [[vulnerability.variables]], [[hazard.variables]] and [[exposure.variables]] entries, see the optional input.



Example
An example of settings file for running a geometry model is given below:
type = "geom"
risk = false
output_dir = "output"

[hazard]
file = "hazard/event_map.nc"

[[exposure]]
file = "exposure/buildings.fgb"

[exposure.variables]
vulnerability = "default"

[vulnerability]
file = "vulnerability/curves.nc"
An example of settings file for running a grid model with combined depth and duration vulnerability datasets is given below:
type = "grid"
risk = false
output_dir = "output"

[hazard]
file = "hazard/event_map_duration.nc"

[[hazard.variables]]
name = "depth"
type = "water_depth"

[[hazard.variables]]
name = "duration"
type = "flood_duration"

[exposure]
file = "exposure/spatial.nc"

[[exposure.variables]]
name = "exposure2"
type = "default"
fn_curve = "struct_2"
vulnerability = ["direct", "indirect"]

[vulnerability]
file = "vulnerability/curves_multi.nc"

[[vulnerability.variables]]
name = "direct"
method = "flood.depth_duration"
types = { depth_direct = "water_depth" }

[[vulnerability.variables]]
name = "indirect"
method = "flood.depth_duration"
types = { days_indirect = "flood_duration" }

title: User guide
text:
Quick start
FIAT computes the (economic) damage and risk of flood events at a specified geographic location based on flood inundation data, exposured assets and vulnerability functions. The model can be configured with a settings file and data inputs:

Settings file
Data

The HydroMT plugin HydroMT-FIAT can be used to set up the FIAT model but that is not compulsory. If a user sets up their own FIAT model, it is recommended to save the data into the same directory structure that HydroMT-FIAT creates.

title: User guide
text:
The models
The data is used by either one or both of the following models:

GeomModel
GridModel

Some more information about the models can be found here.

title: User guide
text:
General User Information
FIAT derives damages and risk at asset-level based on flood maps and additional inputs such as depth-vulnerability curves, asset locations and their maximum values. For each asset specified in the exposure dataset, the water depth or level is sampled from the flood map at the location of the assets.






Note



Water elevations are converted to water depths using the ground elevation of each asset.


See Figure 1 for an overview of the FIAT workflow. To obtain the flood inundation level, FIAT extracts the water depth or level at the location of each asset. For line or polygon assets, either the average or maximum water depth or level and the fraction of the asset are extracted from the hazard map. The inundation depth within buildings or on top of for example, roads, is obtained by subtracting the ground floor height from the water depth. FIAT derives the damage fraction for each asset using its inundation depth and interpolating over its depth-damage curve. Thereafter, the damage to the asset is calculated as the product of the maximum value and the damage fraction. In case an asset is only partially flooded, the damages will be reduced by the dry fraction of the building. Instead of single events, the user can also provide return-period flood maps as input. Hence, FIAT calculates and integrates the associated return-period damages to derive the expected annual damages.






Figure 1: FIAT Workflow. The damage of the flood water level in each object is determined by flood depth-vulnerability curves, which relate the water level to the maximum value of an asset, returning a damage fraction. The damage fraction is multiplied with the max. potential damage to obtain a monetary damage per object.

title: Supported formats
text:
Comma seperated values (CSV)
Your run of the mill csv files. As long as one provides the delimiter in the settings file, anything goes. For example:

comma
semicolon
tab

The amount of columns are determined by length of the header or the first line of data.

title: Supported formats
text:
Geometry files
For geometry files only one file format is supported:

[FlatGeobuf]

Only files containing a spatial index (hilbert r-tree) are allowed. This allowes fiat to quickly index features and batches of features.

title: Supported formats
text:
Gridded data files
Two formats are supported by fiat when it comes to raster (gridded) files.

GeoTIFF
NetCDF

GeoTIFF files are accepted in plain form and in it’s cloud optimized form. NetCDF files need to comply with the GDAL standard for this format. This entails the presense of specific metadata

title: Types of hazard maps
text:
Tip



The most advised format for both event and risk is netCDF.

title: Types of hazard maps
text:
Event
Event maps are generally supplied in singular fashion (i.e. one band per event map). This band just simply contains the hazard values per cell. Let’s have a quick peek at the data:




<class 'netCDF4.Dataset'>
root group (NETCDF4 data model, file format HDF5):
    dimensions(sizes): lat(10), lon(10)
    variables(dimensions): float32 lat(lat), float32 lon(lon), int32 spatial_ref(), float32 data(lat, lon)
    groups: 


<class 'netCDF4.Variable'>
float32 data(lat, lon)
    _FillValue: -9999.0
    grid_mapping: spatial_ref
    type: water_depth
unlimited dimensions: 
current shape = (10, 10)
filling on










Note



Although netCDF is the preferred format, GeoTIFF’s are also very handy for single events.


As one can see, this dataset has only one band (variable).
When created, it is preferred that the event map is compressed to prevent unneccessary data on the hard drive. More information regarding the compression of netCDF files and others settings can be found here.

title: Types of hazard maps
text:
Risk
Risk maps in gerenal should contain multiple bands.
Lets take a look quick look at the data:




/bin/bash: line 1: gdalinfo: command not found










Note



Instead of seeing normal metadata, we only get an overview of the available subdatasets.


Multiple netCDF variables are normally not recognized as bands by the netCDF driver of GDAL. Instead they are interpreted as subdatasets (!). One can set the key var_as_band to true within the settings file to read the subdatasets as bands.
[hazard]
file = <your-file>
risk = true
[hazard.settings]
var_as_band = true
When supplied in one subdataset (all bands are within that subdataset), the subset variable within the settings file should be set under the header hazard.settings. The value set to subset should be the name of the desired subdataset.
[hazard]
file = <your-file>
risk = true
[hazard.settings]
var_as_band = false
subset = <your-wanted-subdataset>

Return periods
The return period of a band is set per band in the settings file with the rp entry of a [[hazard.variables]] entry (required for every band in a risk calculation), see hazard settings. An rp attribute of the band in the file is not read.
Every return period needs a band of every hazard type required by the methods of the linked vulnerability datasets (e.g. a water_depth and a flood_duration band per return period).
Let’s have a quick peek at the data using gdalinfo (it will be at the bottom):




/bin/bash: line 1: gdalinfo: command not found

title: Grid (raster)
text:
Setting
The gridded exposure is a single gridded file (NetCDF advised), set via file under the [exposure] section of the settings.toml. It must have the same grid (resolution, size and projection) as the hazard data, otherwise one of the two is reprojected (see base under [grid]).






Warning



The grid model only supports methods that need no hazard conversion. The method flood.level (water level hazard) can therefore not be used with gridded exposure, see the methods.




Layers
Every variable (layer) with an exposure type in the [[exposure.variables]] entries of the settings file is calculated. The type is set with the type entry and is either:

default: the layer holds the maximum value per cell. The vulnerability curve is set by the fn_curve entry (required); this curve id is looked up in every vulnerability dataset linked to the layer.
categorized: the layer holds a category (integer) per cell, see categorized layers.

Category-value variables must be listed with type = "values" (see categorized layers); they are not calculated by themselves but have their own vulnerability link. Variables of the file without a [[exposure.variables]] entry are ignored (except for the discovery of category-value variables).
The vulnerability dataset(s) of a layer are set by the required vulnerability entry of its [[exposure.variables]] entry, even when it is the dataset named default. A link can be a single dataset or a list of datasets, see linking exposure to datasets.


Categorized layers
A categorized layer <layer> holds a category per cell. Its maximum values are given by one or more category-value variables: 1D variables over a category dimension, by default the variables with the dimension <layer>_cat. Every category-value variable that is used, set with values or found via the dimension, must have its own [[exposure.variables]] entry with type = "values", otherwise FIAT stops with an error. The coordinate of that dimension holds the categories (integers) and the variable holds the maximum value per category. The categories are used as curve ids in every linked vulnerability dataset. Category 0 means no exposure.






Note



The categories are taken from the category coordinate of the category-value variable; the grid itself is not scanned. Cells holding a category that is not in that coordinate produce no damage.


The impact of a cell is the maximum value of its category multiplied by the cell area, taken from the area_sqm attribute of the hazard file (1 when absent).
The vulnerability link of a categorized layer is set on its category-value variables (required, type = "values"); the categorized layer itself has no vulnerability entry. So the category-value variables of one layer may be linked to different datasets. A category-value variable can belong to only one categorized layer.


Settings
The layers, and their attributes, are set in the settings file with a [[exposure.variables]] entry per variable. Attributes of the variables in the file (e.g. type, fn_curve or vulnerability) are not read.
[exposure]
file = "exposure/spatial.nc"

[[exposure.variables]]
name = "exposure2"
type = "default"
vulnerability = ["direct", "indirect"]
fn_curve = "struct_2"

[[exposure.variables]]
name = "exposure3"                        # not in the file: uniform layer
type = "default"
fn_curve = "struct_1"
vulnerability = "default"
value = 1500.0

[[exposure.variables]]
name = "landuse"
type = "categorized"
values = ["exposure_values"]              # category-value variables (instead of the
                                          # '<name>_cat' dimension discovery)

[[exposure.variables]]
name = "exposure_values"                  # category-value variable
type = "values"
vulnerability = ["direct", "indirect"]

name: the name of the variable; it must exist in the file, unless value is set.
type: the exposure type (required): default or categorized for a layer, values for a category-value variable.
vulnerability: the linked vulnerability dataset(s), a name or a list of names (required for default layers and values variables, not allowed for categorized layers).
fn_curve: the curve id of a default layer (required for type = "default").
values: the category-value variables of a categorized layer (only allowed with type = "categorized").
value: a constant value, see uniform layers.



Uniform layers
A [[exposure.variables]] entry with a value defines a uniform layer: a layer that is not in the file and has the same (constant) value over the whole grid. The name must be a new variable (not present in the file) and needs a fn_curve for a default layer. Otherwise FIAT stops with an error when reading the exposure data.

For a default layer the value is the maximum value of every cell.
For a categorized layer the value is the category of every cell; it must be in the category coordinate of the category-value variable(s), set with values.
A category-value variable can not be defined by a value.



Output
The output file holds a band per calculation and hazard identifier (the band number for an event, the return period for risk):

<layer>_<id>: when a layer gives a single calculation (a single dataset, or combined datasets);
<layer>_<dataset>_<id>: when a layer gives several separate calculations. A combined calculation among them is named after its datasets joined by -, e.g. <layer>_direct-indirect_<id>;
total_<id>: the sum of all calculations;
ead: the expected annual damage (risk only).

For categorized layers <layer> is the name of the category-value variable.




 Back to top

title: Exposure data
text: The exposure data describe the assets within the region of interest. FIAT allows vector and raster data inputs. It is recommended to place the exposure data in the ‘exposure’ directory, see the directory structure. However, the file name is free to be chosen by the user and must simply be refered to in the settings.toml configuration file.

title: Exposure data
text:
Types of Data
Because FIAT consists of two models, the exposure data can be supplied in either a vector format or in raster format

Vector data
FIAT can be used to assess flood damages to buildings, roads, utilities, and other types of structures of which data is available. These type of assets are often spatially represented with vector, or geometry data. Building a FIAT model with geometry exposure data requires two data types:

Geometry file(s)



Gridded (raster) Data






Important



This functionality is in beta phase


Raster files must be pre-processed before being ingested into the FIAT model. Raster projection and extent must be coherent among exposure rasters and hazard maps. For each object type (e.g. residential buildings, industrial assets) a layer with the maximum value per cell is required. Each layer refers to a vulnerability curve (fn_curve) in the vulnerability dataset(s) it is linked to in the vulnerability file.

Gridded files

title: Create a container
text:
A container file is present within the repository of Delft-FIAT. This container file can be found here.






Important



We recommend using podman (alternative to docker), the cli calls reflect this.


From this container file an image can be produced. In the creation process of the image, pixi is used. Pixi is a fast(er) alternative of creating and installing python environments compared to mamba (conda). Creating a image can be done with the following command:






Important



The OS running used in the container will be Fedora.








Note



Note: Set the current directory to the directory of the cloned repository.


podman build -f Containerfile --build-arg="PIXIENV=default" -t fiat .
However, as an alternative, it can be build directly from the container file in the github remote repository:
podman build -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Deltares/Delft-FIAT/main/Containerfile --build-arg="PIXIENV=default" -t fiat .






Tip



The build argument PIXIENV is used to define which python enviroment to use. Using the default environment is recommended. An overview of all the environments can be found in the pixi toml file.


After setting up the image, a podman container can be spawned from this image. The podman container will contain all the necessary components to run Delft-FIAT.
To run/ start a podman container from the previously created image:






Tip



The -v argument sets a mount, i.e. connection from a directory on the host machine to the podman container.


podman run -it  -v $PWD/data:/home/deltares/data --name fiat fiat:latest bash
When inside the podman container one can simply call FIAT:
fiat run --help



 Back to top

title: Building FIAT
text:
To build FIAT as an executable/ binary, it is required to clone the FIAT repository to your local drive. This required git to be installed on your local machine.
git clone git@github.com:Deltares/Delft-FIAT.git
Besides pixi (mentioned here), a compiler is necessary as FIAT has extensions written in c++ and cython. MSVC is recommended on Windows and GCC is recommended on Linux. The compiler need to be added to path.
While in the cloned repository, one can install a small python environment used to build FIAT with pixi:
pixi install -e slim
After which FIAT can build be simple calling:
pixi run -e slim build
The resulting build will be placed in the bin/release directory.



 Back to top

title: General information
text:
Delft-FIAT is a free, python-based Fast Impact Assessment Tool, designed and continuously improved by Deltares. It is configured to run quick, consistent, and well-founded flood damage and risk calculations on the basis of flood maps and additional inputs such as depth-vulnerability curves, asset locations, and their maximum values. Delft-FIAT allows rapid assessment of the direct economic and monetary impacts to buildings, utilities, and roads for specified flood events and return periods. Fast impact modeling removes bottlenecks in climate adaptation planning, allowing for large numbers of calculations needed to understand the effectiveness of adaptation strategies and the changes in damage and risk as climate and socio-economic conditions change. In the further documentation, Delft-FIAT will be refered to simply as FIAT.
FIAT works with an easy format for exposed assets, consisting of information on the location, exposed value, ground floor height, and associated depth-vulnerability curves, which can be modified by the user. A simple configuration file specifies the location of depth-vulnerability curves and flood maps, as well as return periods of flood maps if calculating risk.




















Field
Description




1
Hazard
Hazard input: Selected per damage/risk simulation


2
Vulnerability curves
Vulnerability input: Prepared when setting up the model, coupled to exposure objects


3
Exposure data
Exposure input: Prepared when setting up the model, including exposure assets and maximum values


4
Delft-FIAT
Flood Impact Assesment Tool


5
Flood impact
Resulting (economic) damages and risk

title: What’s new?
text:
These are the unreleased changes.



Vulnerability datasets in a NetCDF file: one file can hold several datasets (variables), each with its own calculation method (method) and a hazard type per curve axis (types), both set in the settings
Grid exposure layers can be linked to several vulnerability datasets (vulnerability as a list), either combined in one calculation or as separate calculations, all added to the total
Vulnerability datasets with curves over two or more hazard axes (e.g. depth and duration), interpolated with the new multilinear interpolator InterpND
Methods flood.depth_duration (a water depth and a flood duration dataset combined, grid only) and flood.depth_duration_2d (one 2D depth-duration dataset)
[[vulnerability.variables]], [[hazard.variables]] and [[exposure.variables]] settings to set the attributes of the datasets, hazard bands and grid exposure layers (e.g. method, types, type, rp, fn_curve, vulnerability, values)
Uniform hazard and grid exposure layers from the settings (value in a variables entry): a layer with a constant value that is not in the file (for a categorized layer the value is the category, which must be in the category coordinate)
vulnerability entry per geometry file ([[exposure]]) linking it to a single vulnerability dataset
close method on the models to close the input data





Breaking: the [[vulnerability.variables]], [[hazard.variables]] and [[exposure.variables]] settings are the only source of the attributes of the variables (type, rp, method, types, vulnerability, values, fn_curve). Attributes in the input files are no longer read and variables of the files without an entry in the settings are ignored; the variables of the hazard, vulnerability and grid exposure settings (at least one each), type (hazard and exposure; category-value variables use type = "values" and must always be listed), vulnerability (default exposure layers and category-value variables, not for the categorized layer itself; also required per geometry file; the grid [exposure] vulnerability setting is removed), method and types (vulnerability), fn_curve (default exposure layers) and, for risk, rp (hazard) are required
Breaking: the area_method, impact_type, zonal_method and vulnerability settings of a geometry [[exposure]] entry are moved to its [exposure.variables] table (impact_type can be a single name or a list); the rp setting of [hazard] is removed, the return period is set per band in [[hazard.variables]]
The calculation method is set per vulnerability dataset instead of globally
The method functions have a uniform signature: fn_hazard(hazards, ...) returns a tuple of hazard values and the reduction factor; fn_impact(hazards, exposure, curves, fact)
The hazard types needed (band type) are derived from the methods of the linked vulnerability datasets, so a hazard file can hold bands of several types (e.g. depth and duration)
Geometry risk output column naming: with a single impact type the expected annual damage column is now ead (previously ead_damage); with several impact types there is one ead_<type> column per type
flood.level can only be used with geometry exposure; linking it to a grid layer gives an error








Vulnerability curves are no longer extrapolated: a water depth below the first curve depth gives the first damage fraction (no negative damage) and a depth above the last gives the last (#205)
Column type of the new geometry output columns (written as double, declared as float), which gave garbled output values
Geometry output finalizing could miss the results of the workers, which gave empty output files
Integer hazard bands (e.g. a flood duration stored as int16) are treated as floating point with the nodata value masked, instead of failing in the grid model or using the raw nodata value in the geometry model





CSV vulnerability files; use a NetCDF vulnerability file
The global method setting; the method is set per vulnerability dataset (a leftover method entry in the settings file is ignored)

text:
v0.4.0 (2025-10-28)
Improved CLI and settings file.

Added

Model type (type) and calculation modus (risk) as model properties



Changed

Moved ‘model.type’ (was hazard type) to ‘hazard.type’
Renamed ‘global’ section to ‘model’
Renamed ‘hazard.risk’ entry is to ‘model.risk’ in the settings file
Renamed ‘model.model_type’ to ‘model.type’
Vector reproject chunking now available



Fixed

Better handling of errors during calculations
Check for module specific (e.g. ‘flood’) settings entries
Cli entry overwrite parsing (‘-d’ or ‘–set-entry’)
Default output vector file format (driver) matches input file format
Reading of csv not ending with newline char
Vector reproject dataset creation error

text:

title: Developer guide
text: We welcome contributions like bug reports, bug fixes, documentation improvements, enhancements, and ideas. This guide provided an overview on how to go about it.

title: Developer guide
text:
Development philosophy
The aim of FIAT is to be a lean calculation core, focusing on the main tasks of FIAT of combining exposure, vulnerability and hazard data and calculating damages and risk. Developments related to pre- and post-processing of FIAT data should be done in respectively the HydroMT-FIAT and FIAT Toolbox repositories.

title: Developer guide
text:
Issue conventions
FIAT has known and unknown bugs. Improvements through bug reports or feature requests in our issue tracker are welcomed. Please search open and closed existing issues, before creating a new one.
For issues related to pre- and post-processing of FIAT data, please refer to respectively the HydroMT-FIAT and FIAT Toolbox repositories.

title: Developer guide
text:
Guidelines
Please follow the guidelines when contributing to the FIAT development:

Create an issue if it does not yet exist, when starting contributing. For more information on the issues, see the contributing page.
Fork the repository.
Develop on the repository with descriptive commit messages.
We work with Ruff linting, so always format the added or changed code with this library.
For each newly developed feature we require a pytest test.
Create a Pull Request to the main branch stating the developments made and the related issue.
Once reviewed and if accepted, Deltares will merge the developments to the main branch.

We would like to get in touch with those that want to contribute. Do not hesitate to send us an email [email address coming soon]!

title: Frequently asked questions
text:
How do I install FIAT?
Visit the Setup guide, which provides installation instructions for Windows.


How do I report a bug?
You can submit a new issue with the Bugs template in the FIAT repository. You can also submit an issue regarding Missing or bad documentation, a Feature request, or you can Ask a question.


How do I build a model?
You can use HydroMT-FIAT to build a FIAT model or you can follow the instructions in the User guide.


How do I modify parameters or calibrate my model?
You can manually change parameters (e.g., the Ground Floor Height) in your exposure data in Excel or with Python. You can also use HydroMT-FIAT for this.


How do I request different output?
You can change the output data types in the settings.toml file, visit the Settings file page for more information.


Can I use FIAT for other hazards than flooding?
Yes! If the damage that hazard causes can be estimated in the same manner as FIAT uses for flooding, other hazard maps can be used in combination with corresponding vulnerability curves.


What does FIAT have to do with the car brand FIAT?
Nothing, it is an acronym for Flood Impact Assessment Tool.




 Back to top

title: Models
text: Within FIAT, two types of models are currently present:

title: Models
text:
GeomModel
The GeomModel requires a configuration file that indicates where the exposure geom(s), vulnerability and hazard data are located and whether risk should be calculated on top of damages. The model reads in vector data as exposure assets (e.g., building footprints, road segments, and utility locations) one by one. Each exposure asset gets overlaid with the hazard map and with this data, the corresponding damage fraction is taken from the vulnerability curve and multiplied with the maximum value to get the flood damage. When the user supplies multiple hazard maps with related return periods, they can choose to also calculate risk.

title: Models
text:
GridModel
The GridModel requires a configuration file that indicates where the exposure raster(s), vulnerability and hazard data are located and whether risk should be calculated on top of damages. The model reads in raster data as exposure layers (e.g. commercial, residential, industrial) holding the maximum value values, which should be in the same resolution, size, and projection as the hazard map. To calculate damages, the exposure raster and hazard raster are overlaid and per cell, the maximum value is multiplied with the damage fraction corresponding to the hazard value in that cell. Risk can also be calculated with the GridModel, although it must be noted that this functionality has not been thoroughly tested.

title: Geometry
text:
Setting
A user can specify one or multiple geometry files in the settings.toml. It is advisable to give descriptive names to the geometry files, e.g., buildings.fgb or roads.fgb. Most-used file types are GeoPackages or Shapefiles but more file types are accepted as can be seen at the bottom of this page.






TipExample



Make sure that each geometry file gets it’s own entry in the settings.toml file.


When providing a polygon or line geometry file, a user can choose to use the area extraction method for considering water levels or depths over the whole area of the asset. This can be more appropriate than point estimates for example for large buildings.






Warning



Assets cannot be partially or fully outside the hazard map extent! FIAT will stop if it detects any.


Each geometry file is linked to exactly one vulnerability dataset via the vulnerability entry of its [exposure.variables] table (a single name, required, even when it is the dataset named default). The dataset may hold 1D or 2D curves; its method determines the needed hazard types and columns. Methods that combine several datasets (e.g. flood.depth_duration) can not be used for geometries.
[[exposure]]
file = "exposure/spatial.fgb"

[exposure.variables]
area_method = "area"
vulnerability = "default"

Output
The output geometry file holds, per hazard identifier <id> (the band number for an event, the return period for risk), a column per hazard value of the method (e.g. depth_<id>, and duration_<id> for the depth-duration method), a column per impact column (e.g. damage_structure_<id>) and the total per impact type (e.g. total_damage_<id>). In case of a risk calculation the expected annual damage is added per impact type: a column ead when there is a single impact type, ead_<type> (e.g. ead_damage) per impact type otherwise.


Supported data formats
An overview of supported formats is presented here



Tabular information
In the table down below, an overview is provided od the necessary inputs in either the vector file.



Table 1: exposure input





Field
Required

A more detailed description of the data fields can be found below.

Object Type
The type of the object according to the type of the vector dataset, e.g. occupancy type for a building dataset.


Vulnerability curves
The user can input as many vulnerability curves and related maximum values as required. However, at least one vulnerability curve and related maximum value must be provides per asset. Vulnerability curve column are named as fn_< exposure_type >_< component > (for exposure types, see here). This name can be chosen freely but it is recommended to give it a descriptive name, such as damage (exposure type) in combination with structure or content (components), and it is required to use the same name in the maximum value column. (i.e. max_< exposure-type >_< component >) The value that must be entered is the name of the vulnerability curve, relating to the curve ids of the vulnerability dataset linked to the geometry file in the vulnerability file. Globally, continental vulnerability curves can be obtained from European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, but it is recommended to use more location-specific functions when available.


Elevation
The elevation of the object (e.g. the ground floor height) relative to the surface. It is subtracted from the water depth at the object. Required by all flood methods.


Reference
The reference (height) of the surface compared to the hazard data, e.g. the ground elevation. It is used to convert a water level to a water depth.






Important



Only required for the method flood.level, see the methods.




Maximum value
The maximum value corresponds to the vulnerability curves for each asset. For each vulnerability curve type that was assigned, a maximum value must also be assigned. These values represent the maximum damage to, for example, the structure, content, or other (e.g. inventory). There are methods to derive these values, based on building type and area of the building. Globally, maximum damage values per country can be obtained from European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, but it is recommended to use more location-specific damage values. In the US, FEMA Hazus is an industry standard in how to derive these values.





 Back to top

title: Hazard data
text:
FIAT computes the impact of a flood event or the risk of flooding on a community by using flood maps as hazard input. Flood maps describe the potential flood extent and magnitude in specific geographic areas. Currently, FIAT is only
These flood maps can be obtained from various sources. The The Global Flood Database provides an extensive amount of global flood hazard mapping products.
The user is free to run the model with a variety of flood scenarios, e.g., including mitigation and adaptation measures over a range of future climate conditions, as long as flood maps are available for those scenarios. The flood maps can be either flood elevation or flood depth maps.
With FIAT, the user has the option to assess the impact of a single flood event or the flood risk based on a set of events with multiple return periods. To do the latter, the user must provide multiple hazard maps with the same extent and projection.
In each case, some requirements must be met. The hazard files of any map should be made available as a raster file, see the acceptable file types at the bottom of this page. It is recommended to place the hazard files in the ‘hazard’ directory, see the directory structure. The file name is free to be chosen by the user and must simply be refered to in the settings.toml configuration file.

title: Hazard data
text:
Types of maps
FIAT knows two types of hazard maps:

Event maps
Risk maps

Risk maps are mainly used to calculate the EAD (Estimated Annual Damages). If risk is not set to true in the settings file, the supplied map will be treated as an event map.

title: Hazard data
Hazard data
text:
Settings
The bands that are used, and their type and return period, are set in the settings file with a [[hazard.variables]] entry per band. Attributes of the bands in the file (e.g. type or rp) are not read, and bands of the file without a [[hazard.variables]] entry are ignored.
[hazard]
file = "risk_map.nc"

[[hazard.variables]]
name = "depth_rp10"
type = "water_depth"
rp = 10

[[hazard.variables]]
name = "duration_rp10"                    # not in the file: uniform layer
type = "flood_duration"
rp = 10
value = 3.0

name: the name of the band (variable); it must exist in the file, unless value is set.
type: the hazard type of the band (required).
rp: the return period of the band (required for every band in risk calculations).
value: a constant value, see uniform layers.


Uniform layers
A [[hazard.variables]] entry with a value defines a uniform layer: a band that is not in the file and has the same (constant) value over the whole grid, e.g. a flood duration of 3 days. The name must be a new variable (not present in the file) and, like every entry, must have a type. Otherwise FIAT stops with an error when reading the hazard data.

title: Hazard data
text:
Supported formats
An overview of supported formats is presented here

title: Data
text: FIAT is data agnostic; what you put in is what you get out. Please follow the guidelines in this documentation to build your FIAT model and pay close attention to the validation of data together with local experts.

title: Data
text:
Types of Data
Here a quick overview is given of the required data:

Hazard

Hazard values in a gridded format

Exposure

Exposure data either in vector or gridded format

Vulnerability

Data relating the hazard intensity to damage fraction


These are the types of data that FIAT needs in order to run properly.

title: Data
text:
Directory structure
It is recommended to set up a directory structure as shown below to ensure that FIAT can find each data file and run smoothly. The files inside the directories are example files and do not need to be of those data types or named as such.

├───📁 modeldata/
    |
    ├───📁 exposure/
    │   ├───📄 buildings.fgb/
    │   ├───📄 roads.fgb
    │   └───📄 spatial.nc
    │
    ├───📁 output/
    |
    ├───📁 vulnerability/
    │   └───📄 curves.nc
    │
    ├───📄 hazard.nc
    |
    └───📄 settings.toml

title: Vulnerability data
text:
The vulnerability of an asset is determined by its building type (e.g. ‘residential 1-story building’) and the inundation depth, also refered to as water depth, during a flood event. Different assests incur different degrees of damage at varying inundation levels. This vulnerability can be quantified via flood depth-damage functions, see for example Figure 1. The vulnerability curve relates the water depth to the maximum value per asset and returns the damage fraction (a value between 0 and 1). The damage fraction is multiplied by the maximum value to obtain a damage value. The value of the maximum value differs per asset and must be specified in the exposure data.
Figure 1: Vulnerability curves of different assets/structures.

title: Vulnerability data
Vulnerability data
text:
Methods
The method of a dataset determines which hazard types it needs and how the impact is calculated. The global method setting no longer exists; every dataset carries its own method. The following methods are available:



Table 1: Calculation methods













Method
Datasets per call
Hazard types (bands)
Curve axis types
Impact
Model




flood.depth
1 (1D)
water_depth
water_depth

geom, grid


flood.level
1 (1D)
water_level
water_depth
\(f(d) \cdot E \cdot r\)
geom


flood.depth_duration
2 (1D each)
water_depth, flood_duration
water_depth, flood_duration
\(f_1(d) \cdot f_2(t) \cdot E \cdot r\)

flood.depth_duration_2d
1 (2D)
water_depth, flood_duration
water_depth, flood_duration
\(f(d, t) \cdot E \cdot r\)
geom, grid






Here \(d\) is the water depth, \(t\) the flood duration, \(E\) the maximum value of the exposure and \(r\) the reduction factor of the area method (1 for grid cells).

flood.depth: the hazard is a water depth. For geometries the depth relative to the object is the hazard value minus the elevation column.
flood.level: the hazard is a water level; for geometries it is converted to a water depth with the reference and elevation columns. Because grid calculations do not convert the hazard, this method can only be used with geometry exposure; linking it to a grid layer gives an error.
flood.depth_duration: combines two 1D datasets in one calculation, one with a water_depth axis and one with a flood_duration axis (e.g. a direct and an indirect damage dataset). Both datasets have this method and are linked to the same grid layer, see linking. As a geometry file is linked to a single dataset, this method is only available for grid exposure.
flood.depth_duration_2d: one dataset with 2D curves (water depth by flood duration). For geometries the duration is reduced over the wet part (depth > 0) of the asset.

The hazard file must hold a band of every hazard type that the methods of the linked datasets need, see hazard data.

title: Vulnerability data
text:
Settings
The datasets that are used, their method and the types of their axes are set in the settings file with a [[vulnerability.variables]] entry per dataset. Attributes in the file (e.g. method or type) are not read, and datasets of the file without a [[vulnerability.variables]] entry are ignored. A dataset without a method or with an axis without a type gives an error.
[vulnerability]
file = "curves_multi.nc"

[[vulnerability.variables]]
name = "direct"
method = "flood.depth_duration"
types = { depth_direct = "water_depth" }

[[vulnerability.variables]]
name = "indirect"
method = "flood.depth_duration"
types = { days_indirect = "flood_duration" }

name: the name of the dataset (variable); it must exist in the file.
method: the calculation method of the dataset (required).
types: the hazard type per index dimension (required); the keys must be the index dimensions of the dataset, each one needs a type.







Note



Vulnerability datasets can not be defined by a constant value (as hazard and grid exposure layers can).

title: Vulnerability data
text:
Linking exposure to datasets
Only the datasets linked to the exposure data are used.

Geometry exposure: each [[exposure]] entry (geometry file) is linked to exactly one dataset via the vulnerability entry of its [exposure.variables] table (a single name, required). The dataset may hold 1D or 2D curves. Multiple 1D curves per asset remain handled by the fn_<type>_<component> columns.
Grid exposure: every layer has its own link via the required vulnerability entry of its [[exposure.variables]] entry (for a categorized layer: of its category-value variables). Grid links may be a single name or a list of names.

[exposure]
file = "exposure/spatial.nc"

[[exposure.variables]]
name = "exposure2"
type = "default"
fn_curve = "struct_2"
vulnerability = ["direct", "indirect"]
For a grid layer linked to several datasets, the datasets that share a method combining multiple datasets (e.g. flood.depth_duration) form one calculation with one output; their axis types must be different and together match the method. Every other dataset is a separate calculation with its own output. All outputs of a layer are added to the total. This allows for:

A single 1D dataset (e.g. flood.depth);
Combined 1D datasets, e.g. ["direct", "indirect"] with flood.depth_duration, giving one output;
Separate 1D datasets, e.g. ["default", "other"] with flood.depth, giving one output each;
A single dataset with nD curves (e.g. flood.depth_duration_2d).

A grid layer has a single curve id (fn_curve) that is looked up in every linked dataset. A categorized grid layer uses its categories (integers) as curve ids in every linked dataset. A curve id or category that is not found in a linked dataset gives an error. See grid exposure for more information.






Tip



You can also create vulnerability curves with the HydroMT-FIAT model builder

title: Computational input
text:
The inputs give the user a bit more control over the computational aspects of FIAT.



Table 1: Computational FIAT input settings





Entry
Type
Default




[model]




threads
integer
1

chunk
integer
-


[model.grid]




chunk
list
-












Warning



All settings that are not globally defined (e.g. settings chunk size via hazard.settings) are ill-advised. Please use the global chunking settings.



[model]

threads: Set the number of threads of the calculations. If this number exceeds the cpu count, the amount of threads will be capped by the cpu count.



[model.geom]

chunk: Set the chunk size of the geometry calculations. The calculations will then be done in vectors of these lengths in parallel. This settings will also be used for chunking when writing.







Tip



This input benefits from multiple threads.








Note



This input is only applicable to the GeomModel




[model.grid]

chunk: Set the chunk size for the gridded calculations. This will chunk the data in rectangles with the goal of reducing the memory foodprint. An example would be [1024, 1024,].







Note



This input is only applicable to the GridModel

Model

loglevel: Set the loglevel of the fiat logger from the settings file. Choose from ‘DEBUG’, ‘INFO’, ‘WARNING’, ‘ERROR’ or ‘DEAD’.
risk: In case of a risk calculation this must be set to “true”, for a single events this must be set to “false”.



[projection]

crs: Model-wide projection for the model and the output. If not defined, the projection of the hazard data is used.
force: Whether to force the model-wide projection on all the spatial input files.



[output]

file: The name of the output file. For the geometry model there is an [[output]] entry per [[exposure]] entry; by default the name of the exposure file. For the grid model it is a single [output] section; by default the name of the exposure file with a .tif suffix.



[hazard]

resalg: Method used during resampling/ reprojecting. Default is ‘nearest’, i.e. nearest neighbour.
settings.crs: Projection of the hazard data if it cannot be inferred from the dataset itself.



Variables
The variables of the input data (vulnerability datasets, hazard bands and gridded exposure layers) that are used are specified with a variables entry per variable; at least one entry is required for each of them. These entries are the only source of the attributes of the variables: attributes in the files (e.g. type, rp, method) are not read, and variables of a file without an entry are ignored. Every name must exist in its file, unless the entry defines a uniform layer with value (hazard and grid exposure only). A value entry must name a variable that is not in the file.

[[hazard.variables]]

name: Name of the band (variable).
type: The hazard type, e.g. ‘water_depth’ or ‘duration’ (required).
rp: The return period of the band (required for every band when risk is true).
value: Constant value of a uniform layer that is not in the file.

See hazard data.


[[exposure.variables]]
Only for the grid model.

name: Name of the layer (variable).
type: The exposure type (required): ‘default’ or ‘categorized’ for a layer, ‘values’ for a category-value variable.
vulnerability: The vulnerability dataset(s) linked to this variable, a name or a list of names.
fn_curve: The curve id looked up in the linked vulnerability dataset(s) (required for type ‘default’).
values: The category-value variables of a categorized layer.
value: Constant value of a uniform layer that is not in the file.

See grid exposure data.


[[vulnerability.variables]]

name: Name of the vulnerability dataset (variable).
method: The calculation method of the dataset, e.g. ‘flood.depth’ (required).
types: The hazard type per index dimension of the dataset, e.g. { depth_default = "water_depth" } (required).

See vulnerability data.



[exposure] (geom)

variables.area_method: The method of extracting hazard values based on the exposure geometry. Choose ‘centroid’ or ‘area’.
variables.impact_type: Types of impact, a name or a list of names. This could be monetary damages (‘damage’), affected people (‘affected’) etc.
variables.zonal_method: The method of aggregating the hazard values of an asset when area_method is set to ‘area’. Choose ‘mean’, ‘max’ or ‘min’.
settings.crs: Projection of the exposure geometry data if it cannot be inferred from the dataset itself.



[exposure] (grid)

resalg: Method used during resampling/ reprojecting. Default is ‘nearest’, i.e. nearest neighbour.
settings.crs: Projection of the gridded exposure data if it cannot be inferred from the dataset itself.
